frictionVectors.title: European Gas Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons and remains a key supplier to Europe, but export dependence exposes it to pricing pressure, infrastructure demands, and shifting European energy policy.

frictionVectors.title: Border Instability
frictionVectors.details: Instability in Libya and the Sahel creates persistent security costs along Algeria's southern and eastern borders, while competition among Russia, Western states, and regional actors complicates diplomatic maneuvering.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Infrastructure Footprint
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply involved in Angola's infrastructure and resource-linked finance, giving Luanda useful development capacity but creating long-term exposure to external creditors and strategic bargaining.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Transit
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor strengthens Angola's geopolitical value as a route for copper and cobalt from the DRC and Zambia, but foreign demand and financing may capture much of the corridor's economic upside.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and insecurity moving south from Burkina Faso and Niger are increasing pressure on northern Benin, threatening transport links, agricultural zones, and state control near the frontier.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's economy relies heavily on the Port of Cotonou and regional trade, leaving sovereign economic control vulnerable to Nigerian policy shifts, foreign logistics operators, and cross-border political disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains unusually strong state influence over diamond revenues through its partnership model, but synthetic stones, weaker global demand, and dependence on a narrow export base threaten fiscal resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Foreign interest in Botswana's copper, nickel, and other minerals is growing, creating opportunities for diversification while raising the risk that external firms capture value without sufficient domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The military government has reduced Western security ties and moved closer to Russian security providers, gaining political autonomy but increasing dependence on opaque external military and mining relationships.

frictionVectors.title: Artisanal Gold Leakage
frictionVectors.details: Gold remains a crucial source of state and local revenue, yet informal production, smuggling, and insecurity limit government capture of value and expose mining areas to armed-group influence.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals governance
frictionVectors.details: Gold and rare-mineral activity remains vulnerable to informal trade, opaque licensing, and cross-border smuggling. Limited state capacity reduces Burundi's leverage over foreign buyers and regional intermediaries.

frictionVectors.title: Great Lakes security pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tensions involving eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda continue to constrain border commerce and security autonomy. Burundi's reliance on regional and external partners narrows its room for independent policy.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic-port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port, airport, tourism, and digital infrastructure rely heavily on foreign finance and partnerships. This improves connectivity but leaves critical assets exposed to shifts in European, Chinese, and other external priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic maritime security
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's location gives it importance for fisheries monitoring, shipping, and counter-narcotics operations. External security cooperation is beneficial but can limit independent control over maritime surveillance agendas.

highlights: Oil and logistics remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Oil transport and energy development depend on foreign operators, financing, and regional infrastructure. Revenue volatility and opaque contracting weaken public control over strategic resources.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far North conflicts
frictionVectors.details: Insurgencies and separatist violence disrupt roads, agriculture, and local resource administration. Security dependence on external suppliers and regional partners increases pressure on Cameroon's fiscal and political autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gold and diamond concessions
frictionVectors.details: Formal and informal mining networks operate amid weak state oversight and armed-group influence. Foreign security and commercial actors can gain disproportionate access to concessions and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-resource dependency
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime protection while increasing strategic dependence. This relationship complicates Western engagement and raises concerns over opaque resource agreements.

frictionVectors.title: Oil infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's export system depends on foreign-operated production and the regional pipeline route through Cameroon. Production and revenue controls remain vulnerable to external commercial terms, price shocks, and transit bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Sudan spillover
frictionVectors.details: Conflict around Sudan and continuing militant threats place exceptional pressure on border security and humanitarian capacity. Chad's need for foreign military, financial, and diplomatic backing constrains independent strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: French sovereignty dispute
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to contest France's administration of Mayotte, while migration controls and maritime enforcement constrain Comoros' practical sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Port and connectivity dependence
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on external partners for ports, transport, energy, and telecommunications, limiting domestic control over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms retain major influence in copper and cobalt processing, while Western and Gulf actors seek alternative access and supply-chain leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-linked security crisis
frictionVectors.details: Conflict involving M23 and alleged external backing continues to weaken Kinshasa's territorial control and threatens mining corridors in the east.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependency
frictionVectors.details: State revenues and export capacity remain concentrated in offshore oil, leaving Brazzaville vulnerable to price cycles and foreign operating partners.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction involvement in roads, ports, and industrial projects increase connectivity but can narrow policy flexibility through debt exposure.

frictionVectors.title: Commodity-chain dependence
frictionVectors.details: Cocoa, gold, and emerging critical-mineral sectors remain exposed to foreign traders, processors, and price-setting systems despite efforts to expand domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and security competition
frictionVectors.details: Abidjan's strategic port and northern corridors attract French, Chinese, Gulf, and regional influence while instability in the Sahel raises security and logistics costs.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military concentration
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities provide revenue and bargaining power but make Djibouti highly exposed to rival-power tensions.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: China-linked port and rail infrastructure dominates the economic model, creating strategic leverage and concerns over debt, concession control, and competition with neighboring corridors.

highlights: Suez remains a strategic revenue lifeline

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF-linked reforms and major Gulf investments provide liquidity but constrain policy autonomy over strategic assets and exchange-rate management.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Shipping disruption threatens Suez revenues, while Nile-water tensions with Ethiopia remain a core sovereignty concern.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led energy production
frictionVectors.details: International operators and external technical partners retain major influence over declining oil and gas output, limiting domestic control of the revenue base.

frictionVectors.title: Gas monetization bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Liquefied natural gas and regional gas projects depend on external investment, infrastructure, and offtake markets.

highlights: Red Sea position raises strategic value

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining operations remain central to exports, creating vulnerability to investor pressure, sanctions exposure, and opaque revenue arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Competition among Gulf, Western, and regional actors around Red Sea access increases pressure on Eritrea while limiting its room for independent alignment.

highlights: Sugar and textiles sustain limited autonomy

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, electricity, transport routes, and investment are heavily tied to South Africa, leaving Eswatini exposed to external infrastructure and market decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Preferential-trade vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Sugar and apparel exports depend on external trade preferences and regional supply chains that can be altered without Mbabane's control.

highlights: Conflict continues to erode state capacity

frictionVectors.title: Nile diplomacy confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation but remains a persistent source of tension with Egypt and Sudan.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring, Gulf investment, and Chinese and Turkish infrastructure links provide capital while exposing strategic sectors to external bargaining pressure.

highlights: Transition government courts stronger state control
Oil and manganese remain externally financed

frictionVectors.title: Mining and oil contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-coup authorities are seeking greater national participation and revenue capture, but depend heavily on foreign operators, capital, and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Port and rail dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors around Owendo and mineral rail links remain vulnerable to foreign financing, operator influence, and logistical bottlenecks.

highlights: Senegal remains the indispensable strategic partner
Fisheries and tourism drive sovereignty concerns

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic leverage
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies on Senegal for trade routes, energy connectivity, and regional security, limiting its room for independent infrastructure and foreign-policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries access and enforcement
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing pressure and weak monitoring threaten coastal resource security, while enforcement capacity remains constrained by external funding and equipment.

highlights: Gold and emerging minerals anchor resource strategy

frictionVectors.title: IMF-linked fiscal constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and reform conditions restrict public investment and bargaining power with external creditors, even as stabilization improves macroeconomic control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold, lithium, and illegal mining
frictionVectors.details: The state is pushing local processing and tighter controls, but illegal mining and foreign-linked supply chains continue to erode environmental security and public revenue.

highlights: Junta-led development trades access for speed

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign consortium dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore corridor promises major state revenue and infrastructure, but its financing, logistics, and technical delivery remain dominated by multinational and foreign state-linked partners.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite export concentration
frictionVectors.details: Guinea retains formal ownership of its minerals, yet heavy reliance on foreign operators and raw-ore exports limits domestic value capture and increases exposure to external demand shocks.

highlights: Cashew dependence leaves the economy exposed

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of cashew trade
frictionVectors.details: Exporters and external buyers capture much of the value from the cashew economy, while limited processing capacity leaves producers vulnerable to price and logistics disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Port, security, and narcotics vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions and limited maritime enforcement create openings for illicit networks and foreign influence around ports, shipping, and coastal security.

highlights: Ports and minerals gain strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and reliance on external lenders constrain Nairobi's room to negotiate infrastructure, energy, and logistics arrangements. Chinese, Gulf, and Western financing compete for influence around ports, transport corridors, and digital networks.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and transport corridor remain vulnerable to militant attacks, local grievances, and delays in associated infrastructure. Insecurity raises the cost of turning the corridor into a sovereign regional trade asset.

frictionVectors.title: Water Sovereignty and South African Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Lesotho Highlands Water Project provides vital revenue and strategic leverage, but its infrastructure and market are heavily dependent on South Africa. Construction delays, compensation disputes, and security around dams can expose asymmetries in bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Industrial Volatility
frictionVectors.details: Diamond mining and export-oriented manufacturing bring foreign capital but remain vulnerable to commodity cycles and external market decisions. Limited domestic processing reduces the country's ability to capture more value from its resources.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Large mining concessions generate jobs and fiscal receipts but leave Liberia exposed to foreign operators, commodity-price swings, and disputes over land, royalties, and local procurement. Weak domestic processing limits sovereign value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Influence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and surrounding logistics infrastructure attract competing external commercial and strategic interests. Limited state capacity makes concession transparency and long-term control persistent sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security authorities continue to contest control over oil installations, export routes, and revenue allocation. Production interruptions and opaque distribution weaken national sovereignty over the core strategic resource.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military and Energy Footprints
frictionVectors.details: External states and private military networks retain influence through security partnerships, bases, arms relationships, and energy deals. This internationalizes domestic disputes and limits Libya's ability to set independent infrastructure and export policy.

highlights: Energy and logistics gaps constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Nickel, Cobalt, and Mineral Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed mining projects provide export earnings but concentrate infrastructure, processing, and marketing power outside Madagascar. Fiscal, environmental, and community disputes can erode public legitimacy and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Energy Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity and limited port capacity increase dependence on external financiers and operators for strategic infrastructure. This weakens bargaining power when negotiating mining logistics, power supply, and major transport projects.

frictionVectors.title: IMF Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed reforms are narrowing fiscal policy space, while external creditors retain substantial leverage over public investment and procurement.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Input Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Fuel, fertilizer, and electricity shortages expose Malawi to import-price shocks and external infrastructure financing, limiting control over agricultural and energy security.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The junta relies heavily on Russian security assistance while reducing Western involvement, creating opaque arrangements around military access, mineral security, and political influence.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Contestation
frictionVectors.details: State efforts to increase control over gold operations confront multinational mining interests, artisanal mining networks, sanctions exposure, and persistent insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Project
frictionVectors.details: The Senegal-Mauritania offshore gas project offers major revenue and energy leverage but leaves both states exposed to foreign operators, export infrastructure constraints, and cross-border governance disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Stakes
frictionVectors.details: Large European- and Gulf-linked hydrogen proposals could diversify the economy, but land, water, transmission, and offtake agreements may lock in external control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Settlement Implementation
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is seeking to convert its sovereignty gains over the Chagos Archipelago into effective administrative and maritime control while managing the strategic role of the Diego Garcia facility.

frictionVectors.title: External Hub Competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, Gulf states, and Western partners compete for influence over ports, digital connectivity, and financial services, requiring Mauritius to preserve regulatory and strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting diplomatic recognition of its autonomy plan into investment and infrastructure support, while legal and political opposition continues to challenge resource projects in the territory.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Technology Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Renewables, electric-vehicle supply chains, ports, and defense modernization strengthen Morocco's leverage but also create exposure to European, Chinese, Gulf, and US technology and capital.

highlights: Cabo Delgado Remains the Sovereignty Test

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique still relies heavily on Rwandan and regional forces to contain the insurgency threatening LNG assets in Cabo Delgado. This limits independent control over the country’s most strategic resource corridor.

frictionVectors.title: LNG Revenue and Local Grievances
frictionVectors.details: External energy companies dominate capital, technology, and project management, while local communities remain concerned about displacement, employment, and revenue distribution.

highlights: Critical Minerals and Green Hydrogen Push

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of New Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: International firms are positioned to lead offshore oil, uranium, and green-hydrogen development. Namibia is seeking stronger domestic participation and fiscal terms before large-scale projects mature.

frictionVectors.title: Export Infrastructure Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, power, and water constraints could leave Namibia dependent on foreign infrastructure finance and limit its leverage over mineral and energy exports.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The junta is pursuing greater control over uranium and other extractive assets while challenging longstanding foreign commercial arrangements. Production uncertainty and legal disputes could still reduce near-term state revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Corridor Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Regional isolation, border tensions, and disrupted trade corridors constrain access to fuel, finance, and export routes. New security ties with Russia and fellow Alliance of Sahel States members offer alternatives but do not replace lost infrastructure capacity.

highlights: Gas and Critical Infrastructure Under Strain

frictionVectors.title: Oil Theft and Multinational Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, pipeline vandalism, and weak enforcement continue to erode public control over petroleum revenues. International operators retain major technical and financial leverage despite regulatory reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Gas Infrastructure Deficits
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, gas-supply constraints, and damaged transport infrastructure restrict industrial sovereignty. Foreign capital remains essential for LNG, refining, transmission, and major logistics projects.

highlights: Disciplined State, Externally Exposed Supply Chains
Great Lakes Minerals Drive Regional Pressure

frictionVectors.title: DRC Conflict and Mineral Allegations
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda faces persistent accusations that networks linked to its security interests benefit from mineral flows associated with eastern DRC conflict. International scrutiny threatens trade access and diplomatic room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: Aid and Security Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda maintains substantial influence over domestic development and security policy but remains exposed to donor pressure and external financing conditions. Its overseas security deployments also generate reputational and fiscal risks.

frictionVectors.title: GULF OF GUINEA EXPLORATION
frictionVectors.details: International companies retain interest in São Tomé and Príncipe's offshore blocks, but limited discoveries and weak state capacity constrain bargaining power. Contract transparency and revenue management will determine whether exploration strengthens sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: FISHERIES AND MARITIME SURVEILLANCE
frictionVectors.details: The country has limited capacity to monitor its exclusive economic zone, leaving fisheries vulnerable to foreign pressure and illegal activity. External maritime-security assistance is useful but increases dependence on outside partners.

frictionVectors.title: OIL AND GAS CONTRACTS
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production has increased Dakar's leverage, while the government seeks greater local participation and closer review of legacy agreements. Renegotiation risks friction with international operators and could delay investment.

frictionVectors.title: FISCAL AND INFRASTRUCTURE DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and financing needs leave major infrastructure and energy projects reliant on external lenders and contractors. Fiscal consolidation may constrain the government's ability to convert resource revenues into broad domestic development.

frictionVectors.title: TUNA ACCESS AND FISHERIES CONTROL
frictionVectors.details: Foreign industrial fleets remain central to the tuna economy, creating recurring tension over access fees, local value capture, and enforcement. Seychelles must balance revenue needs with long-term control of its marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: MARITIME SECURITY COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: The archipelago's position in the western Indian Ocean draws security and infrastructure interest from India, China, the United States, and European partners. Port, surveillance, and logistics cooperation can improve resilience but risks strategic overdependence.

highlights: Mining remains the central sovereignty test

frictionVectors.title: IRON ORE AND MINING CONCESSIONS
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale mining continues to anchor exports while foreign operators control much of the capital, technology, and logistics chain. Revenue-sharing, environmental impacts, and domestic processing remain persistent sources of political friction.

frictionVectors.title: CHINESE INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-linked financing and construction are important for roads, ports, and industrial projects, but repayment obligations and limited local procurement can reduce national value capture. The government is seeking investment without surrendering excessive policy autonomy.

highlights: Maritime sovereignty is becoming a national priority

frictionVectors.title: ETHIOPIA-SOMALILAND PORT DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Somalia's opposition to external arrangements involving Somaliland reflects a broader struggle to preserve territorial and maritime sovereignty. The dispute risks regional escalation and complicates cooperation with Ethiopia on trade and security.

frictionVectors.title: TURKISH SECURITY AND ENERGY ROLE
frictionVectors.details: Turkey has become a major security and maritime partner, supporting defense capacity and potential offshore energy development. This strengthens Mogadishu's position but also creates dependence on a single external actor amid weak domestic institutions and continuing al-Shabaab threats.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CAPITAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial regulatory leverage over platinum, manganese, and other minerals, but aging infrastructure and policy uncertainty leave extraction and processing dependent on foreign capital and technology.

frictionVectors.title: LOGISTICS CONSTRAINT
frictionVectors.details: Rail and port failures are reducing export sovereignty, benefiting competing regional corridors and weakening Pretoria's ability to capture value from mineral exports.

frictionVectors.title: PIPELINE VULNERABILITY
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's oil exports depend on infrastructure crossing conflict-affected Sudan, exposing revenue and production to Sudanese battlefield dynamics and foreign operators.

frictionVectors.title: RESOURCE GOVERNANCE
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation, opaque oil arrangements, and armed patronage networks limit state control over petroleum revenues and deepen dependence on external security and commercial partners.

frictionVectors.title: GOLD WAR ECONOMY
frictionVectors.details: Competing armed actors and cross-border trading networks are using gold to finance the conflict, weakening formal state control and increasing exposure to external sponsors and buyers.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND TRADE ACCESS
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan and key transport routes remains strategically contested, while disruptions are increasing leverage for foreign states and commercial intermediaries over essential imports and exports.

frictionVectors.title: PORT CONCESSION POLITICS
frictionVectors.details: Expanded foreign participation in port and logistics infrastructure is intended to increase trade capacity but has generated domestic concern over long-term control of strategic gateways.

frictionVectors.title: LNG AND MINING TERMS
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking better fiscal and local-processing terms in natural gas and critical-mineral projects, while major investors retain significant bargaining power over timelines and technology.

frictionVectors.title: PORT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional trade position, but reliance on foreign logistics, finance, and shipping networks limits full national control over corridor revenues.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY SPILLOVER
frictionVectors.details: Militant pressure from the Sahel is raising security costs around northern transport routes and increasing reliance on external security assistance and intelligence partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: European financial and diplomatic support remains closely tied to Tunisia's role in controlling irregular migration. This limits Tunisian policy autonomy while intensifying domestic criticism of external conditionality.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported hydrocarbons and constrained investment in renewables leaves Tunisia exposed to external price and financing pressures. Declining phosphate performance further weakens export leverage.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline could expand state revenue and export capacity, but financing constraints and international opposition over environmental and human-rights concerns increase reliance on politically aligned investors.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, energy, and industrial projects strengthen Uganda's infrastructure base while creating long-term exposure to foreign contractors, debt servicing, and resource-linked commercial terms.

frictionVectors.title: Copper Ownership and Value Capture
frictionVectors.details: Rising copper demand gives Zambia greater negotiating power, but foreign-controlled mines, tax disputes, and limited domestic refining constrain the country's ability to capture full strategic value.

frictionVectors.title: Creditor and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms are stabilizing the macroeconomic position but narrow policy flexibility. Dependence on regional transport corridors also exposes mineral exports to external infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms, particularly from China and other Asian markets, remain central to investment in lithium, platinum, and other minerals. Zimbabwe is seeking beneficiation, but financing needs and governance concerns limit domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Monetary and Sanctions Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, restricted access to international finance, and persistent sanctions-related friction weaken state economic sovereignty. The government consequently relies heavily on mineral revenues and politically aligned external partners.
